bc_revelstoke.blurb: Revelstoke sits in the Columbia Mountains of interior British Columbia, with the Selkirk and Monashee ranges as its backdrop. The climbing is overwhelmingly single-pitch sport, with a smaller block of waterfall ice, mostly WI3 to WI5, and only a handful of trad lines. Sport grades run from about 5.6 up through 5.12, with the heaviest concentration around 5.10 and a solid supply of 5.8 and 5.9 for building up. Roadside cragging on quartzite is the staple, and Begbie Bluffs is the biggest and most varied cliff, ranging from very easy terrain to the low 5.13 range, though rock quality there is uneven. Shaketown, The Shire and Blanket Canyon are other names worth knowing. Alpine granite routes also exist higher in the mountains.

md_patapsco_valley_state_park.blurb: Patapsco Valley State Park follows the Patapsco River for roughly 32 miles, southwest and west of Baltimore, and its climbing is scattered between several separate sections of the park rather than gathered in one place. Bouldering makes up most of it, followed by top-rope lines and a smaller number of trad and sport routes. Boulder problems run from very easy up to about V10, with the bulk between V0 and V6, while the roped climbs mostly fall between 5.6 and 5.11. Sub-areas to know include Alberton, Woodstock Rock and Ilchester, plus boulder clusters such as Gorsuch Switch and the Bloede Dam Boulders. It is a modest, local-scale destination rather than a big-name crag region.

bc_nelson.blurb: Nelson sits on the Kootenay River in the Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia, and the climbing is spread over granite and gneiss outcrops around town and along the roads toward Ymir and Salmo. Sport routes lead and trad is a close second, with only a sprinkling of boulder problems. Grades center on the 5.9 to 5.11 range, with a solid supply of moderates and a handful of harder lines. The largest cluster is the CIC (Fairview) Bluffs, followed by Ymir Swimming Hole, Kootenay Crag and Hall Siding. Routes range from single pitches to multi-pitch outings, and many crags sit near water for a swim afterward. The season typically runs from April to October, and the area is drier than Squamish and cooler than Skaha.

mt_east_side.blurb: The east bank of the Gallatin River in Gallatin Canyon, south of Bozeman, holds a string of gneiss buttresses reached by trails climbing away from the river. Most of the climbing is traditional, with a small bundle of sport routes at spots like Northern Exposure. Grades center on 5.10 and 5.11, with a healthy number of 5.8 and 5.9 routes and a hard tail into 5.12 and 5.13. The style is tricky and almost alpine in feel, mixing cracks, chimneys, grooves and some fourth-class scrambling, with exposure and runouts common higher up, so carry more gear and clothing than seems necessary. Skyline Buttress is the largest, followed by Black Line Buttress, The Waltz Formation and Sparerib Area. Many routes see little traffic.

ca_mickey_s_beach.blurb: A coastal climbing zone just south of Stinson Beach in Marin County, where the Pacific sets the mood: ocean breeze, surf noise, and fog that can leave holds slick. Sport routes make up the bulk, mostly 5.10 to 5.12 with some 5.13, plus a smaller group of moderates and a little trad. Bouldering is the second draw, spanning V0 to well into double digits, with a good spread of easy to mid-grade problems. The Main Rock and Vent 5 hold much of the roped climbing, while Danger Rock and the boulders on the Stinson Beach side cover the problems. Smaller walls such as Kim's Gym, The Egg and Motown fill in the middle. The setting is scenic, and dolphins and porpoises are often seen offshore.

ab_jasper_national_park.blurb: Jasper National Park in the Alberta Rockies offers a mixed bag of crags spread around the townsite and along the highways nearby, with a few ice and alpine objectives on the side. Sport climbing dominates, mostly single-pitch, with a modest share of trad. Grades center on 5.7 to 5.10, with real depth in 5.10 and a harder tail through 5.12, so beginners and strong leaders both find something. The largest sectors are Cinquefoil, Watchtower Creek, Lost Boys and Morro, followed by Hidden Valley, Juno Wall and Rock Gardens. Morro Slabs is a limestone wall beside the Athabasca River. Crags sit at differing elevations and faces, and winter is quiet apart from visiting ice climbers.
